title: The Transformer
oneLiner: The Transformer drops recurrence entirely: stacks of attention and small feed-forward networks process every word at once, and the same design now powers chatbots, translators and image models.

what.html:
A Transformer is a stack of identical layers, each with two parts: an attention step where every token gathers information from the others, and a feed-forward step where each token processes what it gathered. Shortcuts (residual connections) and normalisation keep the deep stack trainable.

Everyday versionA meeting where everyone can hear everyone at once (attention), followed by each person quietly thinking it over (feed-forward), repeated for several rounds. After a few rounds each person's understanding reflects the whole room, not just their neighbour.

It comes in three flavours: an encoder that understands text, a decoder that writes text one token at a time, or both together for translation-style tasks.

why.html:
• RNNs read one word at a time: slow to train and forgetful over long texts.
  • Attention connects any two words directly and processes all positions in parallel on GPUs.
  • That parallelism made it practical to train on trillions of words, giving LLMs such as GPT, Claude, Gemini and LLaMA.
  • The same architecture works for code, images (ViT), speech and proteins.

how.title: Three architectures for three jobs
how.html: Encoder-only (BERT): every word sees every other word, great for understanding: classification, named entities, extractive QA. Decoder-only (GPT, Claude, LLaMA): each word sees only earlier words, great for generating. Encoder–decoder (T5, BART): read the whole input, then write a different output: translation, summarisation.

how.title: Words in, vectors out
how.html: Each token (a word or word piece) is looked up in a table to get a vector of, say, 512 numbers. A positional encoding is added so the model knows which word came first, since attention alone ignores order.

how.title: Attention: tokens talk to each other
how.html: Multi-head attention lets every token look at every other token, with 8–12 "heads" each looking for different kinds of relationships. In "river bank" vs "bank account", the word "bank" ends up with a different vector because it listens to different neighbours.

how.title: Feed-forward: each token thinks alone
how.html: After the exchange, each token goes through the same small two-layer network on its own: expand to 4× the width, apply a non-linearity, shrink back. This is where most of the layer's parameters live.

how.title: Normalise and add a shortcut
how.html: Before each step, layer normalisation rescales each token's vector to a standard range. After each step, the original input is added back (residual connection), so each layer only learns a refinement and gradients have a highway through deep stacks.

how.title: Stack it, and count the cost
how.html: Repeat the layer N times (6 in the original, 12 in BERT-base, 96 in GPT-3). Each encoder layer has about 12 × d² weights: d = 768 gives about 7 million per layer, and BERT-base totals about 110 million including its word table.

how.title: The decoder: write without peeking
how.html: The decoder has three steps per layer: masked self-attention (each word sees only earlier words, so training matches word-by-word generation), cross-attention (look at the encoder's understanding of the source sentence), and the feed-forward step. A final layer scores every word in the vocabulary, and softmax picks the next word's probabilities.

how.title: Images as sentences of patches (ViT)
how.html: Cut a 224×224 image into 196 squares of 16×16 pixels, turn each into a vector, add a special [CLS] token and position information, and run an ordinary encoder. The [CLS] vector at the end summarises the image for classification. ViTs need lots of pretraining data but transfer extremely well; CNNs win on small datasets.

how.title: How each variant is pretrained and used
how.html: BERT learns by filling in hidden words ("The [MASK] sat on the mat" → cat). GPT learns by predicting the next word. T5/BART learn by repairing corrupted text. During training the decoder predicts every position at once (with the mask); when generating, it produces one token, appends it, and repeats.

how.title: Pretrain once, fine-tune many times
how.html: Pretraining on terabytes of text is expensive, so we download a pretrained model (e.g. from Hugging Face) and fine-tune it on a few thousand labelled examples with a tiny learning rate (about 0.00002) for 2–5 epochs. Judge it with the right metric: accuracy/F1 for classification, exact match for QA, BLEU/ROUGE for generated text.

how.title: LoRA: fine-tune a giant cheaply
how.html: Instead of changing all the model's weights, freeze them and learn a small add-on made of two thin matrices (B × A). For BERT-base that's about 0.3 million trainable numbers instead of 110 million, with similar accuracy, and the add-on can be merged in afterwards so the model runs just as fast.

demo.html: Press Play (or Step) to follow "this book" through the encoder and "yeh kitab" through the decoder, one sub-layer at a time, with the shape of the data at each stage.

example.html:
Translation "this book" → "yeh kitab" (encoder–decoder). Named entities "Teddy was US President" → [PER, O, LOC, O] (encoder-only). Completion "The weather today is" → "sunny and warm with a gentle breeze" (decoder-only). Fine-tuning BERT on 25,000 IMDb reviews for sentiment.

Supplementary A telecom operations team fine-tunes a small encoder on a few thousand labelled trouble tickets to route them to the right team, and uses a decoder-only LLM with retrieval over runbooks to draft resolution steps; LoRA adapters keep one base model per language with tiny task add-ons.

misunderstandings: Transformers generate all words at once.
Training is parallel, but generation still adds one token at a time.
Positional encodings are concatenated to embeddings.
They're added element-wise (same size), despite one slide's wording.
The decoder only looks at the encoder.
It also attends to its own earlier outputs (masked self-attention).
Only with large pretraining; on small datasets CNNs usually win.
Fine-tuning needs a big learning rate to change the model.
Use about 2e-5; large rates wipe out what pretraining learned.
takeaways: A Transformer layer = (LayerNorm → multi-head attention → add) + (LayerNorm → feed-forward → add), stacked N times.
Encoder: bidirectional, ≈12d² weights/layer. Decoder: masked self-attention + cross-attention + FFN, ≈16d²/layer; output linear + softmax.
Encoder-only (BERT, MLM) to understand, decoder-only (GPT, next-token) to generate, encoder–decoder (T5, BART) to transform.
ViT treats 16×16 patches as tokens with a [CLS] token and learned positions; needs large pretraining.
Pretrain once, fine-tune with small LR (2e-5–5e-5) for 2–5 epochs; LoRA trains <1% of weights.
thirty: The Transformer replaces recurrence with attention. Each layer has a multi-head self-attention step, where every token gathers information from every other token, and a position-wise feed-forward step, each wrapped with layer normalisation and a residual connection; layers are stacked N times. Encoders are bidirectional and suit understanding tasks; decoders add a causal mask, plus cross-attention to an encoder in seq2seq models, and generate one token at a time through a linear and softmax output. That gives three families: BERT-style encoders trained by masked language modelling, GPT-style decoders trained to predict the next token, and T5 or BART encoder–decoders. Vision Transformers apply the same encoder to image patches. In practice you take a pretrained model, for example from Hugging Face, and fine-tune it with a small learning rate, or with LoRA to train under one percent of the weights.

check.q: What problem of RNNs does the Transformer most directly remove?
opts: Sequential processing that prevents parallel training
check.why: Self-attention processes all positions at once.
